title: French factory orders improve as firms struggle to pass on costs
summary: French industrial output improved in October, yet capacity use edged down and manufacturers reported difficulty passing higher costs on to customers. The Banque de France survey points to concentrated demand for defence equipment, aircraft and data-centre infrastructure alongside much thinner orders elsewhere. It also helps date the information correctly. About 8,500 companies and establishments were interviewed between 28 October and 4 November. The original French release appeared on 9 November. The bank published the English translation on 17 November. The information was already public by then.

The industrial activity balance reached +5 in October, and respondents expected +6 in November. These figures are percentage-point balances between firms reporting improvement and deterioration. They do not mean that output rose 5% or that a 6% increase was expected. Capacity utilisation was 76.6% after 76.7% in September, and inventories of finished goods were still high. Those observations can coexist with a positive activity balance. An order for aircraft components can add to activity in a high-demand sector while stock accumulates at a car manufacturer struggling to sell existing output. Composition matters before drawing a conclusion about the output gap or the need for new capacity.

Order books were particularly well filled in aeronautics and computer, electronic and optical products. Demand associated with electrification, defence and digital infrastructure also supported electrical equipment. In contrast, automotive and machinery orders deteriorated, while chemicals, non-metallic mineral products and wood, paper and printing reported thin books. Part of the October recovery in electrical equipment followed September supply disruptions. Part of the prospective November improvement in pharmaceuticals involved clearing a backlog. Both can raise production temporarily without a matching improvement in final demand. In transport equipment and in computer, electronic and optical products, about one-quarter of firms still reported supply difficulties.

The price evidence shows that an input shock can arrive before firms can recover it in cash. Energy, metals, circuit boards and packaging all appeared in company comments. Competition and existing contracts constrained selling prices. Twelve percent of industrial firms raised prices in October, against 8% in a typical October. Thus repricing remained unusually frequent for the month even though it slowed relative to earlier reports. Ten percent expected to raise prices in November. In market services, 9% raised prices against a 6% seasonal norm, while the November expectation was about 7%, close to normal for that month. Fuel costs could pass through immediately in transport, whereas some temporary-work and business-service prices fell. These are frequencies of repricing, which cannot be read as average price changes.

Cash positions remained weak in both industry and market services. Manufacturers described slower customer payments, and cash balances deteriorated further in cars and chemicals while improving in electronics and aeronautics. Services growth also concealed a shift in hiring preferences. Firms used temporary staff as uncertainty made them reluctant to take on permanent employees. Construction activity was broadly flat because finishing work offset weaker structural work. The text-based uncertainty indicator rose sharply in construction, where some customers postponed decisions and firms already faced weak order books. Across sectors the share reporting recruitment difficulty fell to 15%. The raw sector readings on page 5 are revealing. Recruitment difficulties affected 23% of construction firms against 14% in each of industry and market services. Building firms could struggle to fill particular roles even as housing and public-sector orders weakened. Their ability to pass costs on appeared limited: 9% raised quoted prices in October and 10% expected to do so in November, both broadly in line with their seasonal averages. These figures measure different groups of respondents and cannot establish that the builders facing hiring difficulties were those raising prices. The uncertainty index on page 4 is derived from managers’ free-text comments, with 100 as the normal reference level. Its rise in construction signals heightened concern. The evidence of delayed projects comes from the accompanying comments.

The Banque de France expected moderate French GDP growth in the fourth quarter, combining the survey with INSEE indicators and higher-frequency information. It published no precise growth rate for the quarter in this release. One forecast error is immediately measurable: the preceding survey had suggested a 0.1% rise in third-quarter GDP, while INSEE’s first estimate showed a 0.1% decline after a flat second quarter. That 0.2 percentage point difference sets a useful scale for interpreting the direction of the latest estimate. A better November industrial balance could improve the quarter, but weakness in construction, pressure on margins and the uneven breadth of services demand limit how much can be inferred from that single indicator.

questions.question: Are manufacturers absorbing the energy shock or merely delaying price increases?
questions.detail: Track the next reported frequencies of industrial repricing alongside producer input and output prices, distinguishing firms constrained by existing contracts from transport firms with rapid fuel pass-through. Check subsequent cash balances and payment times. A rise in repricing after contracts turn over would indicate a lag. Continued weak margins with flat selling prices would favour absorption through profits.

questions.question: Do stronger orders forecast production beyond the sectors tied to defence and data centres?
questions.detail: Compare the industrial survey balance with first-release INSEE production by sector. Construct weights using information available at the time and repeat the comparison without the sectors reporting unusually strong books. Check inventory movements and the clearing of pharmaceutical backlogs. A rebound confined to those sectors would give less support to broad fourth-quarter improvement.

questions.question: Does greater use of temporary labour signal strength or deferred permanent hiring?
questions.detail: Compare temporary-work activity, reported recruitment difficulties and subsequent temporary and permanent hiring data. Separate accommodation, engineering and construction, where prospects differ. The survey’s explanation predicts relatively resilient temporary hiring and slower permanent commitments, especially in sectors where uncertainty and postponed orders were rising.
